title: Olympiad for People with Disabilities, Day 6: Poland takes sole lead
summary: With just one round remaining at the 3rd FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities, the competition entered its decisive stage in Samarkand. Poland produced a commanding 4-0 victory over the Czech Republic to emerge as the sole leader heading into the final round, while Day 6 also put the spotlight on clean sport, fair play and the measures that help ensure equal conditions for everyone at the chessboard. The day carried additional significance as competition at the 46th FIDE Chess Olympiad also got underway in Samarkand. For the first time, the Olympiad for People with Disabilities is being held alongside the Open and Women’s Olympiads, bringing players from across the chess world together in the same host city. Before the clocks were started for Round 6, the ceremonial first move was made by Nigel Short, FIDE Director for Chess Development, marking the beginning of the penultimate round. For participants in the 3rd FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities, the proximity of the events has created opportunities to meet some of the world’s leading players, visit the main Olympiad, and experience the atmosphere of one of chess’s biggest events – while competing under comparable professional playing conditions themselves. Day 6 also welcomed a delegation from Abu Dhabi, UAE, as preparations are already looking ahead to the next editions of the events in 2028. Mohsin Al Hashmi, Shaikha Alzaabi and Qasaed Altamimi visited the venue to observe the organization and gain first-hand experience ahead of the 2028 Chess Olympiad and the 4th FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities, which will take place in Abu Dhabi. Their visit offered an opportunity to see the event operations in practice, from the playing conditions and accessibility arrangements to the overall organization of the competition, as preparations for the next Olympiad cycle continue. Clean sport: Fairness beyond the chessboard Alongside the battles over the board, Day 6 focused on another fundamental part of competition: clean sport. Anti-cheating measures are already an established part of top-level chess, but the Olympiad has also featured anti-doping controls, adding another dimension to the principle that sporting success should be based on a player’s own skill, preparation and hard work. Dorian David, a representative of the Classification Commission at the event, explained that conducting anti-doping controls for players with disabilities required particular preparation and attention. “It was a challenge because testing people with disabilities is not easy at all. But I can tell you that there weren’t any problems.” David also highlighted the importance of Therapeutic Use Exemptions (TUEs) for players who require medication containing substances included on the prohibited list. He stressed that players are responsible for the substances present in their bodies and should ensure that the appropriate procedures are followed when medication requires an exemption. For David, however, clean sport ultimately comes down to something much broader than testing. “Clean sport is about fair play. And fair play… is winning through hard work. It’s also about respect – valuing your opponent, valuing the rules, respecting the rules.” A different kind of Fair Play challenge Fair Play Officer Jürgen Klüners described working at the Olympiad as a particularly distinctive experience. Klüners, who was previously in Samarkand as an arbiter at the Grand Swiss, explained that fair play procedures at an event for players with disabilities sometimes require officials to adapt their usual approach to individual circumstances. “Being a Fair Play Officer in this championship is very, very special, because we are checking people and all these people have several problems, and so it’s completely different to, let’s say, a normal Chess Olympiad or other championships.” For him, patience and understanding are essential when carrying out the necessary checks while respecting the individual needs of every participant. Klüners also emphasized the significance of staging the Olympiads alongside one another. Players at the event have access to professional conditions familiar from other major FIDE competitions: electronic boards, clocks, live results, media coverage and a full tournament infrastructure. “We have more or less the same playing conditions. You see these screens with the results; they play with DGT boards with normal clocks. You have press officers giving interviews. So I think these people really appreciate this.” Chess has been a lifelong part of Klüners’ own story. A player who once reached a rating above 2200, he began working as an arbiter at youth tournaments at an early age. Today, alongside his work as an arbiter and Fair Play Officer, he serves as Vice President of the German Chess Federation and continues to play team chess. “You have to use your own prowess, talent or hard work” The meaning of clean sport was equally clear to Kenya’s Ronny Otieno. “It’s very important because it levels the field. You have to use your own prowess, talent or hard work to succeed. So clean sport is good for the sport.” For Otieno, returning to the Olympiad has also been about friendships and shared experiences. Having participated in the previous edition in Kazakhstan, he spoke warmly about meeting players from other countries and praised the hospitality and organization in Samarkand. The presence of the main Olympiad has added another memorable dimension. Otieno said he had already encountered several stars of world chess, including Vasyl Ivanchuk, Praggnanandhaa Rameshbabu and Gukesh D. His own journey in chess began at the age of nine, when a childhood friend taught him the game. Initially chess was simply for fun, but years later, while at college, friends encouraged him to test himself in tournaments. “I used to claim I’m the best. I never knew there were better people than me. So I started coming to tournaments, and since then it’s been fun. I mean, this is the best space anyone can ever be.” Vietnam makes its Olympiad debut For Thuy Thi Bich Tran, Samarkand represents a milestone: Vietnam is participating in the FIDE Chess Olympiad for People with Disabilities for the first time. “It’s the first time Vietnam can get on the list for the Olympiad, so

title: Samarkand Olympiad Day 1: Favourites, fireworks and a shock
summary: The opening round produced dominant victories for the favourites, colourful scenes around the venue and an unexpected defeat for India’s Arjun Erigaisi. The 46th Chess Olympiad got underway this afternoon in Samarkand, Uzbekistan, with 207 teams registered in the Open section and 191 in the Women’s section. As is often the case in a Swiss-system event, most of the higher-rated teams started their campaigns with victories, although the opening round also produced a few surprises. Let’s take a closer look at the action from the playing hall. Following a brief introduction by the tournament’s Chief Arbiter, Ivan Syrovy, the action began punctually at 3 p.m. local time with two ceremonial first moves. First, Viswanathan Anand, five-time World Champion and FIDE Interim President, opened with 1.c4 on board one for Jamaica’s Joshua Christie, who faced Uzbekistan’s top player, Nodirbek Abdusattorov. Immediately afterwards, officials and media moved a few meters to board one in the Women’s section, where hosts Uzbekistan faced Trinidad & Tobago. On this occasion, Alisher Sadullaev, First Vice President of the Uzbekistan Chess Federation, played 1.e4 as his ceremonial first move for Uzbekistan’s Gulrukhbegim Tokhirjonova, who faced Shemilah James. With the round officially underway, the players shook hands, and the games began. With almost 200 four-board matches taking place simultaneously, there was certainly no shortage of action to follow. A walk through the playing hall allowed me to exchange a brief head nod with World Champion Gukesh (!), reacquaint myself with many players, coaches, and arbiters and, perhaps most importantly, admire the colourful outfits being sported by teams from around the world. It is customary for teams to wear a T-shirt, polo shirt, or tracksuit top featuring the name and colours of their country, but some have taken things a step further, with players’ names printed on the back. The Women’s section offered an even greater variety of designs and traditional attire – and, fittingly, a special prize will be awarded for the best-dressed team. I was particularly impressed by the Mozambique team’s outfits, which will surely make them strong contenders for this particular prize. After all, the Olympiad is not only about chess; it is also about bringing together players, traditions and cultures from all corners of the world. Hundreds of spectators have been arriving from all over Uzbekistan to follow the games. The organisers have created a huge space known as the EXPO, cleverly connected to the exit of the playing hall. Once their games are finished, players can mingle with spectators, sign autographs and pose for photographs, while fans can follow the remaining games with Grandmaster commentary on a giant screen. This creates a natural meeting point between players and fans and adds another dimension to the Olympiad experience beyond the playing hall. Returning to the games, most of the top teams won their opening matches comfortably, with several recording convincing 4–0 victories. Interestingly, a number of teams chose to rest one of their top boards: a decision that can have various explanations, from travel and health considerations to tournament strategy. Top seeds, the United States were among them. Fabiano Caruana sat out the opening round, leaving Wesley So to lead the team to a convincing 3½–½ victory over Iraq. The only half-point dropped by the Americans came on board three, where Levon Aronian was held to a draw. Making his debut for the United States at an Olympiad, Hans Niemann produced a crushing 23-move victory on board two. Afterwards, he joined Charlize van Zyl for a brief interview, where he revealed a new team-building activity that has apparently become part of the American squad’s routine. When asked who the best player was, Niemann had a typically confident answer: “Padel will speak for itself!” https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=-Tr4Xmnqm1w Other teams chose to field their top stars from the outset. Argentina, for example, opted for a fascinating strategy, with 12-year-old Faustino Oro leading the team despite being the lowest-rated member of the squad. So far, the decision has paid off handsomely. Argentina defeated Kenya 4–0, with Oro producing a convincing 22-move victory on the top board. Even though most of the rating favorites went through the round comfortably, Botswana played a fantastic match against Brazil, achieving a 2-2 final score. A major upset, given that the African country was outrated by more than 400 points per board.  The biggest upset of the day came on board one, where Thailand’s Prin Laohawirapap scored a stunning victory with the Black pieces against India’s top board, Arjun Erigaisi. The result meant that the defending champions had to settle for a 3–1 victory over Thailand. Erigaisi had enjoyed the better position for much of the game, but a tactical oversight towards the end allowed Laohawirapap to turn the tables and secure a memorable win. With both players running short of time, Erigaisi faced an extremely tricky position. He needed to find 50.Qf4!, defending against Black’s numerous threats around his exposed king while keeping his extra pawn and some winning chances. Instead, Erigaisi blundered with 50.Qg7??, allowing the decisive sequence 50…Qh1+ 51.Kg4 Re4+ 52.Rf4 Qd1+, when his king was caught in a dangerous crossfire between the black queen and rook. The game continued 53.Kg3 Qg1+ 54.Kh3 Re3+, and Erigaisi resigned. A remarkable turnaround: after being in control for much of the game, the Indian star was suddenly unable to escape the combined attack of the queen and rook. Charlize van Zyl caught up with the delighted winner in the interview area shortly afterwards. https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1bv2zotXh6o In the Women’s section, the rating gap between some of the teams was even more pronounced than in the Open, and Round 1 produced a large number of clean sweeps. Among them were all five top seeds: India, Georgia, Kazakhstan, China, and the United States. Even so, converting an advantage into a point is never straightforward, as Uzbekistan’s Umida Omonova discovered in her game against Trinidad & Tobago’s Zara La Fleur.
